Please check again in 5 minutes.” The note stays in the system on their device, and the system automatically retries every 5 minutes for up to 30 minutes. If it still fails after that, the system shows a second message: “Still unable to send. Please contact IT now.”

The system shows a message when ShareSheet is unreachable and retries every 5 minutes for 30 minutes. The system shows a contact-IT message and sends an alert to IT after 30 minutes of failure. The nurse never loses the note and knows exactly what to do.
The system must also prevent nurses from editing a note after 48 hours — once it’s been synced, it’s final, unless a supervisor approves a correction.
The system should flag any edit after 48 hours and send it to the team leader for review.
If a note isn’t entered by 10 a.m. the next day, it stays in the system as a pending task for the nurse, but the team leader gets an alert at 10:15 a.m. with the nurse’s name and patient full name.

When the ward manager opens the system each morning, the first thing they see is a summary dashboard with three key items: the number of notes entered so far today, how many are overdue (more than 10 a.m.), and a list of nurses who haven’t entered a note yet.
The manager then sends a quick message through the system to the nurse — no phone calls needed — saying “Hi, just checking in on your notes for Mr. Smith. Thanks!”
If a nurse has missed two notes in a row, the manager gets a yellow alert and can schedule a quick 5-minute huddle to check in.
If they’re new to the system, they get a short video pop-up the first time, but only once.

The team leader gets an alert at 10:15 a.m. with the nurse's name, the missing patient, and the time. The alert includes a direct link to the note entry page. The alert shows nurse name, patient full name, note type and due time on one line, red, pinned to the top.
If the note still isn’t entered by 9:30 a.m., the system escalates it to the ward manager automatically.
as a care coordinator, I want to see a clear indicator of which notes are urgent or require immediate action — like a red tag for new assessments, medication changes, or falls
if a note is missing, I want it to be obvious — not just a blank row, but a red highlight with the patient’s name and the time it was due

when a nurse saves a ward note in InHealth, the system must immediately confirm the note was sent to ShareSheet, with a clear message on screen. If the send fails, the system must retry automatically every 5 minutes for 30 minutes...

the status line must update in real time, without needing a refresh. If the connection comes back after 12 minutes, the nurse should see “Sent” appear automatically on the same screen, right after the “Retrying” message

They need to see the dose, the unit (like mg or mL), and the time the medication was given—those three details are critical. They also need to confirm the patient’s bed number and MRN are correct before saving—those are auto-filled from Epic but must be visible for double-checking.
The first thing a nurse does when they start a shift is open the tool from their tablet, log in with their NHS smartcard

New medications are flagged for review by the ward manager the next day. The patient’s bed number and MRN are auto-filled from Epic and visible for double-checking.
Every note creation and edit is logged once. The log includes nurse ID, timestamp, and action type. The log is stored read-only for seven years.
The ward manager's list will include medication flags for new entries, so they can review them the next day.

Letting nurses enter observations first—those are the most frequent and time-sensitive updates, especially blood pressure and heart rate, which need to be recorded at the start of each shift. The pain score is also critical for patient care and often missed during retyping.

Heart rates above 200 should trigger a warning, as they’re extremely rare and likely a typo. I’ll also set a limit for temperature: anything above 45°C or below 30°C should show a warning. For blood pressure, systolic above 250 or below 80, and diastolic above 150 or below 50, should be flagged. ... a warning will help catch input errors without stopping the nurse.
Saving with a blank pain score is blocked. The system should show a clear message: “Pain score is missing—please enter a value before saving.”
I’ll make sure the form includes clear fields for each observation, with dropdowns or numeric inputs to reduce errors.

The tool must hold the note in progress—either by auto-saving every few minutes or by prompting the nurse to confirm before closing. We can’t allow the system to lose work, especially during a pilot where reliability is key.

The pass test is one full shift on the pilot ward with every note entered once, in the tool, with no retyping into SharePoint. We’ll need three clean shifts in a row—no double entry, no major errors, and all notes successfully saved and visible in the handover file. ... Ward manager confirms each time that the notes match what they see in the EPR and the spreadsheet.

Only mismatches that delay handover count as major errors—like a medication dose that’s wrong and causes a nurse to stop and verify it, or a missing pain score that leads to a patient being reassessed. ... If a nurse has to re-enter a note because the tool crashed or closed unexpectedly, it counts as a double entry and fails the pass test.

If Epic is unreachable during submission, the note is immediately persisted to our Azure SQL Database with a status of “Pending” and a retry queue is triggered via Azure Service Bus. The system automatically retries the FHIR POST every 30 seconds for up to 15 minutes, with exponential backoff.

Only the pharmacy liaison and the charge nurse can open an alert-flagged note, and each access is logged in Azure Monitor with the user ID, timestamp, IP address, and the note’s MRN. When the liaison opens the note, they must select a reason from a dropdown.
